course: AI literacy — What is a computer that learns? (ages 7–9)
topic: Teaching a computer with examples (patterns, machine learning, a first trained model)
audience: Year 3–4 class (ages 7–9); mixed ability; one hour computing / AI-literacy slot; no prior coding
learningOutcomes: Sort a mixed set of objects or pictures into categories and explain the rule they used.
Describe machine learning in three steps: give examples, find patterns, make a prediction about something new.
Train a two-class model in Teachable Machine (or equivalent), test it on a new example, and say what changed when they used few examples versus many.
Give one example of the model getting something wrong and explain that it only knows patterns from the examples it was shown.

sections.title: Hook: a machine that seems to know you
sections.purpose: Activate everyday experience of recommendations or face unlock without treating that chat as proof of understanding.

sections.title: We sort; computers need many examples
sections.purpose: Make pattern-and-classification visible with a hands-on sort so later training talk has a concrete landing pad.

sections.title: Three steps: examples, pattern, prediction
sections.purpose: Give a shared, sayable model of machine learning before any tool is opened.

sections.title: Lab: train a two-class model
sections.purpose: Each pair actually trains and tests a model so the idea is something they did, not only something they heard.

sections.title: Few examples, many examples, and a mistake
sections.purpose: Show that quality and number of examples change the prediction, and that a wrong label is a pattern gap, not magic failing.

sections.title: Individual check-out
sections.purpose: Collect one independent spoken or written account per learner; pair work does not count as individual evidence.
